Two VLCCs were struck INSIDE the southern corridor Admiral Cooper publicly declared cleared on Aug 28, and Iran separately claims a sea-mine strike. The framework is actuarial, not political: reopening is decided by war-risk underwriters pricing incident frequency in a specific lane over a specific quiet period, and an attack inside the declared-safe lane resets that clock regardless of what any president offers. Base rate is the Tanker War of 1984-88, where traffic recovered only after a ceasefire plus convoying and never during an attack series. Dated falsifier stands: no attack on a laden tanker in the international lanes through Sept 22 plus a published minesweeping calendar scores this a MISS and sends the number back toward 21

hypotheses.name: The Iran file is coalition-captured (NEW — the capture read, tracked as opinion)
hypotheses.d: The claim: on the Iran file, organized coalition pressure — donor networks, primary structure, allied commitments, defense-institutional momentum — outweighs the base's war fatigue, which is why a 'no more wars' White House struck anyway and now substitutes sanctions for settlement rather than sign a visible retreat before the midterms. Mechanisms named, plural: status clock vs electoral clock, sunk cost after declaring victory, lobbies as veto players that raise the price of defection (one interest group among several — any single-key version of this hypothesis is scored separately and currently rejected). Opens at 70%: the strike itself, the 6-month grind, and 'not in a hurry' all fit; capped because the same facts also fit ordinary planning failure plus vanity. Falsifier: a signed de-escalation or negotiated Hormuz reopening BEFORE the midterms — the base's clock winning on the party's most captured file would kill the strong form outright.

hypotheses.name: The IRGC, not Mojtaba, rules Iran (working model) — 75% → 82%
hypotheses.d: Week's biggest mover, on three strands independent of the Israeli/exile channel. Pezeshkian said on Iranian state TV that communication with Khamenei is 'very difficult' — Tehran's own president, against his own interest. Washington routed its peace offer not to Araghchi but to Mohsen Rezaee, career IRGC commander-in-chief now running the security council. Cipher Brief: 'Tehran isn't saying who is actually in charge.' Capped at 82% because the state has promised footage of Mojtaba meeting commanders — that is the falsifier, and it is coming.

hypotheses.name: Nobody’s hurrying on Hormuz — HELD at 60%
hypotheses.d: The near-breakthrough-then-condition pattern fired a sixth time (Iran–Oman interim corridor and 30–60 days of technical talks, against Ghalibaf restating the full condition stack). Deliberately not moved: it is already priced, and a minesweeping calendar is what an honest process looks like too. The real test is live — the offer sits with the IRGC, so Tehran's answer is the experiment.

hypotheses.name: Détente as harvest cover — 55% → 60%
hypotheses.d: The discriminating split signal arrived: PLA sorties kept declining while the coast guard escalated in kind — CCG 2307 pressing a Japanese coast guard ship in the strait Aug 6–10, which AEI reads as testing whether foreign vessels will obey PRC authority. Kinetic down, jurisdiction up is the ratchet signature. Capped at +5; the stated tell is what the coast guard does through the Sept 24 visit.

hypotheses.name: NEW · Venezuela was a Hormuz hedge in a drug-war uniform
hypotheses.d: The clearest revealed-preference play on the board — and the reason it opens at 55 rather than higher. Sturdy mechanism first: US Gulf-Coast refineries are plumbed for heavy sour crude, Venezuela sits on the planet's largest heavy reserves, and moving that barrel north through the Caribbean to Texas and Louisiana structurally hedges the one risk that ran live all year — a Hormuz closure. The Aug 28-29 deal (a new operator taking control of ~65bn barrels, about a fifth of Venezuela's reserves) is exactly what this hypothesis predicts, and the reporting frames it in plain words as an alternative to Gulf oil routed through Hormuz. So oil-as-motive is near-certain. What is NOT settled — and what caps this — is premeditation: was Operation Southern Spear a counter-narcotics and regime-change campaign that harvested the oil after the fact, or an oil-security operation in a drug-war uniform from the start? The tell against design is the clock — the deal trailed Maduro's Jan 3 capture by eight months, which reads more like spoils than master plan. Mundane alternative, named and live: drugs, migration politics, regime-change, with the barrel a bonus. Falsifiers — cut hard if export volumes stay token (the $2-2.8bn tranches are a rounding error against control of 65bn bbl), if Gulf-Coast heavy sourcing does not actually swing off the Middle East, or if the fixed infrastructure (GEO-022) never appears. One correction the excitement needs: a canal cannot bypass Hormuz, geography does not work that way — the hedge is source substitution plus Caribbean routing, not a waterway. Real Orinoco or Maracaibo channel-dredging and dedicated heavy-crude terminals WOULD be the premeditation tell. Unconfirmed today; it is the thing to watch.

hypotheses.name: US drift hardened into leverage play — 45% → 52%
hypotheses.d: Economic Outcast hit ~60 teapots, tankers and traders and touched no Chinese state major and no bank — Treasury sent the majors a warning letter instead. Maximum pressure on Iran, calibrated to stop exactly short of anything that would detonate the Sept 24 summit. Held to +7 because the Munir offer is a real concession, and $4.10 gas before midterms is real evidence against premeditation.

hypotheses.name: NEW · A pre-announcement leak into oil futures
hypotheses.d: Four times in the war window, nine- and ten-figure short bets landed 15–20 minutes before an Iran announcement: ~$2.2bn across crude, gasoil and gasoline before Trump's Mar 23 pause post; ~$950m before the Apr 7 ceasefire; ~$760m before Iran said Hormuz would open. ~$7bn total; CFTC probing, four members of Congress demanding answers. Split: deliberate leak 45 / mediator-side 20 / skilled opportunism 25 / coincidence 10. This is the only entry in the book whose evidence is timestamped BEFORE the event rather than pattern-matched after — which is why it opens this high. Against it: no episode has surfaced around this week's diplomacy.

hypotheses.name: Moscow shapes Tehran's maximalism — 30% → 25%
hypotheses.d: Cut again. The channels that actually moved this week were Oman, Pakistan and the new Mecca defence pact — Russia was absent from every one of them, and still has not offered the mediation this hypothesis expects. Motive 9/10, documentary evidence 0/10, pre-event evidence never. Cut to 15% if nothing surfaces by Sept 30.

hypotheses.name: War pause was secretly packaged with the Beijing summit — on the retirement line
hypotheses.d: Both its live predictions came in favourably this week and it gets credit for neither: the rival leverage hypothesis predicted the same things, and shared predictions are ambience. One more failed pre-summit call and it goes to the epitaph list.

brief.head: Iran retaliates against US bases in Jordan, Kuwait and Bahrain
brief.h: CENTCOM struck air defences, radars, maritime assets and the Hormozgan power network at Bandar Abbas, Qeshm, Sirik and Jiroft airport; Iran answered with 13 ballistic missiles at a US base on Jordan's Gulf of Aqaba coast, of which Jordan's military intercepted 10, plus drones intercepted over Kuwait and a claimed strike in Bahrain - and a US strike on a house hosting a wedding in Kuhestak killed five people including a child and wounded at least 68, the deputy governor of Hormozgan province said.
brief.t: The board's read all week has been that this war climbs two or three rungs and then stops below an American death, and it did that again - but the shape of the retaliation changed. Iran did not answer American hulls with American hulls; it put missiles and drones over Jordan, Kuwait and Bahrain, which means the physical cost of Tehran's response is being paid by three governments that are not party to the fight and that host the bases. That is the point of the choice: it manufactures pressure on Washington through allies who must now explain their air defences to their own publics, without crossing the one line that would compel an American answer. CENTCOM's line that the US military never targets civilians met five dead at a wedding on the same afternoon, which is the standard collision between a precision claim and a target list that includes a provincial power network.
brief.context: Name the mechanism: host-state cost transfer, the way a weaker party answers a superpower by charging the bill to its allies. The rail predates the crisis - the same forward-basing architecture that lets CENTCOM fly from Jordan and Bahrain is what makes those countries the cheapest place for Iran to aim, and it is why the Gulf states spent the years after 2019 quietly hedging with Tehran. The deciding desks on the retaliation side are Jordanian and Kuwaiti air defence and the Bahraini palace, not the White House podium. The base rate inside this six-month war remains unforgiving to escalation forecasts: every exchange since February has climbed and then stopped short of an American death, and this one stopped there too. What would change the read is not a bigger sortie count but a host government publicly restricting American operations from its soil.

angles.effect: Gains a demonstration of escalation dominance at no American cost, and keeps the threat priced without spending it - the biggest attack of them all is described as still waiting in the wings
Gains a retaliation it can show at home while keeping every impact below the American-casualty threshold, which is what preserves its control of the tempo
Pay the entire physical cost - interceptors, closed airspace and the domestic politics of being shot at for hosting somebody else's war
Pay in the gap between a precision claim and a target list that includes a power network: five dead at a wedding in Kuhestak, at least 68 wounded

dec.kill: An American killed or a US-flagged hull struck - the published trigger on this board, still unfired; or a host government formally restricting US strike operations from its territory, which would end the cost-transfer play.

consp.claim: That Iran has already killed a large number of US forces in the Jordan salvo and the casualties are being suppressed.
consp.spread: A 326-reply /pol/ thread that shot to the top of the catalog within hours, running alongside the standing Persia Israel General now on its 2013th thread
consp.read: The suppressed-casualties frame, and it attaches to exactly the variable everyone knows is load-bearing - our own board publishes an American death as the escalation trigger, which makes a claim that one has already happened the highest-value rumour on the table. The checkable kernel is thin: Jordan says it intercepted 10 of 13 and no wire has reported a US casualty. The frame is self-sealing, because absence of confirmation is read as proof of the cover-up rather than evidence against the claim.

brief.head: Germany blames Russia for Leipzig drone and shuts Bonn consulate
brief.h: Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said police investigations, patterns of the offences and intelligence findings together establish Russian responsibility for the explosive-laden drone found and defused beside a Ukrainian cargo aircraft at Leipzig/Halle on 4 August, flown by agents acting on behalf of Russian state entities; Berlin summoned the ambassador, is closing Russia's consulate general in Bonn and the Russian House in Berlin, and will push for EU sanctions, travel restrictions on Russian nationals and more pressure on the shadow fleet, while NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said the evidence is clear.
brief.t: Read the target, not the airport. Leipzig/Halle is one of Europe's largest air-freight hubs and the routine waypoint for the An-124, the outsized-cargo aircraft chartered to move military equipment, and the device was found beside a Ukrainian plane - so the object under attack was the logistics rail into Ukraine, at its cheapest point. The more telling number is the four weeks between the incident and the attribution. Attribution is not a discovery, it is an instrument: governments hold it until the response package is assembled, and Berlin released the finding, the summons and the consulate closure on the same afternoon. Moscow's foreign ministry called it an anti-Russian action it would answer, which is the reply of a state that has priced the exchange and finds it affordable.
brief.context: Name the mechanism: attribution as a scheduled weapon. The rail predates the headline - Germany has had the machinery to expel diplomats and close consulates since the Tiergarten expulsions, and the shadow-fleet and visa measures were already drafted inside the EU sanctions process, so what arrived today is a permission slip rather than a new capability. The deciding desks are the BfV and BKA on the evidentiary side and the Auswaertiges Amt on the response, not the podium. The base rate is the discipline here: every European attribution of a Russian hybrid operation since 2024 - Poland, the Baltic cables, the incendiary parcels in air freight - has produced expulsions, listings and closures, and not one has produced an Article 4 consultation, let alone Article 5. What would move that is a fatality on NATO soil, not another finding.

angles.effect: Converts an unsolved four-week-old incident into a dated, visible response, and pre-frames the domestic argument for defence spending without having to publish its evidence
Loses a consulate general and a cultural centre, and gains confirmation that an explosive device on NATO soil costs it two buildings and no Article 4 consultation
Gains the political attention and none of the protection - the freight hub is no harder to reach tonight than it was on 4 August
Pay through tightened border controls and travel restrictions applied to a population rather than to the agents the finding names

dec.kill: Publication of the evidentiary basis, or an arrest, would move this from asserted to established. A symmetrical Russian expulsion with no further incident would confirm both capitals are managing this as diplomacy rather than escalation.

consp.claim: That the attribution is the opening move of a conscription push - that the finding was timed and framed to prepare German and European publics for a draft and emergency powers.
consp.spread: A 209-reply /pol/ thread headed with a direct call to get ready for conscription and built on an OSINT account's post, running beside a 198-reply thread headed simply that it is over for Germany
consp.read: The manufactured-consent frame, arriving at exactly the threshold moment it always attaches to. The checkable kernel is real but thin - four weeks from incident to attribution, no suspect in custody, no published evidence - and the frame converts that gap into intent. It is durable precisely because European conscription debates are genuinely live, so nothing short of a decade cleanly falsifies it.

brief.head: Trump summons refiners as diesel closes on $6 a gallon
brief.h: The president met at least ten fuel makers and distributors, among them Marathon Petroleum, Chevron, Delek US and PBF Energy, pressing them to raise gasoline and diesel output and discussing permitting, regulation and further investment - at a moment when US refineries have been running at 97.4 per cent of operable capacity, the longest sustained stretch near the limit in more than 25 years, with diesel near $5.60 a gallon and up roughly $2 on the year and gasoline at $4.10 against $3.19 a year ago.
brief.t: There is nothing in the room to summon. A refining system at 97.4 per cent utilisation has no spare capacity to be talked into, which makes this a meeting about a physical wall rather than a negotiation about willingness - and it is the clearest sign yet that the Hormuz shock has finished travelling from the barrel to the pump. The distinction that carries the story is crude versus crack: sanctions and diplomacy can move the price of oil, but the American diesel price is set by refining capacity the US spent 2019 to 2021 closing. The levers that would actually move it are not in the refiners' hands at all. They sit with the EPA, in blending and fuel-specification waivers, and with the option nobody has said out loud - restricting distillate exports.
brief.context: Name the mechanism: the refining bottleneck, where the binding constraint on a fuel price is not the oil in the ground but the plant that turns it into diesel. The rail predates the crisis - roughly a million barrels a day of US refining capacity closed between 2019 and 2021 and never came back while demand did, so the system has run with no margin for a supply shock since well before this war started. The deciding desk is the EPA fuels office and the Department of Energy, not the podium and not the chief executives. The base rate is discouraging for the announcement: presidential refiner summits have been run before, and the June 2022 letters to seven refiners produced neither higher utilisation nor lower pump prices inside a quarter, because utilisation was already the constraint then too. What would change the read is an actual instrument - a signed waiver, or an export limit.

angles.effect: Gains a visible act on the one number voters feel weekly, two months before the midterms, without having to name the tools that would work or own their costs
Gain the strongest crack spreads in years plus a live conversation about permitting and regulatory relief, and concede nothing binding in a closed-door meeting
Pay now - diesel is a freight input, so a $2 move on the year is an inflation transmission line into every delivered good, and heating oil follows it into winter
Would pay if the export lever is pulled - American distillate exports are what keeps their diesel balanced, so an export restriction exports the shortage

dec.kill: An EPA fuel-specification or blending waiver, or any restriction on distillate exports, would show the administration reaching for the real instrument. Refinery utilisation falling below 95 per cent while pump prices stayed high would show slack existed and the constraint was never physical.

brief.head: G20 backs US text on trade imbalances with China alone dissenting
brief.h: Two days of finance ministers and central bank governors in Asheville, North Carolina closed with a statement every member but China backed in full, holding that excessive and persistent imbalances pose risks and can generate economic distortions; Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said getting 19 to agree showed the sheer enormity of the problem and urged counterparts to use tariffs as his administration has, while Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov attended in person for the first time since 2022, over European complaints.
brief.t: Two trades ran through one communique. The United States used its G20 presidency to convert a bilateral tariff fight into multilateral language about Chinese overcapacity - which is what Europe has wanted on paper for a decade - and in the same room readmitted Russia's finance minister for the first time since the invasion. Allies got the sentence; Washington got the precedent. The load-bearing caveat is that a G20 communique binds nobody. It is a permission slip a government can cite later when it imposes a measure of its own, which is exactly why 19 signatures are worth more to Bessent than the text itself, and why Beijing loses very little by refusing to sign a thing that constrains nobody who does.
brief.context: Name the mechanism: communique laundering, where a plurilateral sentence is manufactured now so a national measure can be presented as consensus later. The rail predates the headline - the G20 has been arguing about imbalance language since the 2010 Seoul indicative-guidelines fight, which produced a formula and no policy change in any surplus country. The deciding desk is Treasury international affairs and the sherpa channel, not the leaders. The clock matters more than the text: the leaders' summit is 14-15 December at Doral, the tariff truce with Beijing is still standing and a Trump-Xi meeting sits on 24 September in between, so nobody in Asheville had an interest in breaking anything. What would change the read is a member other than the United States actually citing this language to justify a measure.

angles.effect: Gains 19 signatures on the premise behind its tariff policy, and a multilateral frame for measures it intended to take regardless
Pays reputationally as the sole dissenter and concedes nothing binding - a communique it did not sign constrains it less than one it did
Get the overcapacity language they have sought for years, and pay for it by sitting in a G20 room with Russia's finance minister for the first time since 2022
Gains the most valuable item on the table without signing anything - readmission to the room, which is the precedent that outlives the text

dec.kill: A G20 member other than the United States imposing a trade measure that explicitly cites the Asheville imbalance language would make it an instrument. The December Doral summit passing with no member acting on it would confirm it as a press release.

brief.head: Energy secretary heads to Caracas to unveil the Venezuela oil deal
brief.h: Energy Secretary Chris Wright travels to Venezuela this week and Chevron is expected to sign an expansion agreement on Wednesday, as US officials defended a structure under which the Defence Department holds a 35 per cent stake and the State Department the right to buy 20 per cent of output at cost, across a 100-year lease on 17 large fields holding roughly 65 billion barrels operated by North American Blue Energy Partners under Alejandro Betancourt - approved by Venezuela's National Assembly, where lawmaker Luis Emilio Rondon abstained and demanded the full and complete text of what had been agreed.
brief.t: The most useful sentence in the story is Rondon's: the legislature that just approved the treaty has not read it. That is the caveat protocol in one line - what has been announced is an approval, what is missing is the instrument, and until the text is published nobody outside the negotiating room can say what governing law, arbitration seat or sanctions authorisation sits under a hundred-year lease. Then watch which cabinet officer flies. An energy secretary going to Caracas to unveil a structure whose equity sits at the Defence Department is the ceremony that turns a term sheet into a signed thing, and the fact that a security ministry holds the shares is the part that will still matter in ten years, long after the barrel count has been forgotten.
brief.context: The distinction that carries this is control versus title: a 35 per cent stake in a venture plus a right to buy a fifth of output at cost is cheap barrels and influence, not ownership of reserves in the ground, which stay Venezuelan under Venezuelan law. Time-to-delivery is the second constraint - these are extra-heavy grades needing diluent, upgrading and a power system that currently fails, so incremental barrels are a multi-year capex story rather than a next-quarter one. The deciding desks are OFAC on the sanctions authorisation and the US Gulf Coast refiners on whether the grade is wanted, not the podium in Caracas. The base rate on century-length concessions signed with unelected interim governments is poor: they get renegotiated or expropriated at the next political shock, which is why the arbitration seat in the unpublished text is worth more than the reserve figure in the press release.

angles.effect: Gains revenue, sanctions relief and the legitimacy of being the counterparty Washington signs with - which is what an unelected interim president most needs
Gains a heavy-crude hedge against Hormuz and a pre-midterm price story, booked as costing the taxpayer nothing, which means no appropriation this year rather than no sovereign risk
Gains a hundred-year operating position with government equity sitting beside it, which is the cheapest political-risk insurance available anywhere
Pay the option - a century-long lease signed by an interim administration removes the choice from everyone who comes after, and whoever funds development carries the expropriation risk

dec.kill: Publication of the full legal text with governing law, arbitration seat and the named sanctions authorisation would settle what was actually signed. Rondon's demand going unanswered through the signing would confirm the instrument is being withheld from the body that approved it.

lesson: In June 1914, weeks before the war, Winston Churchill stood up in the Commons as First Lord of the Admiralty and asked Parliament to buy 51 percent of the Anglo-Persian Oil Company. The argument was not commercial. He had converted the Royal Navy from Welsh coal to oil for speed, and in doing so had made the fleet dependent on a liquid Britain did not produce - so the state bought the producer rather than trust the market to sell to it in a crisis. That is the rail under today's Venezuela announcement, and it is worth naming precisely: a defence ministry taking an equity position in a foreign oil venture is not an investment, it is a supply guarantee bought with a balance sheet instead of a contract, and it appears whenever a military finds its fuel on the far side of somebody else's chokepoint. The Pentagon's Office of Strategic Capital holding 35 percent of a Venezuelan venture, with a right to buy a fifth of the output at cost for the reserve and the military, is Churchill's instrument with the serial numbers filed off. What the precedent predicts is the part nobody announces on day one. State equity creates a state obligation to defend the asset, and it converts every subsequent local political change into a foreign-policy problem: APOC's stake bought Britain fuel for two wars and then bought it Mossadegh's nationalisation in 1951 and a coup in 1953, because a century-long claim on another country's principal resource outlives the government that granted it. So here is the falsifiable version rather than the cautionary tale. If this is a supply guarantee in the Churchill mould, the fixed infrastructure follows the equity - awarded dredging, a dedicated heavy-crude terminal, upgraders - because barrels you own but cannot move are not a guarantee; if eighteen months pass with the stake in place and no funded logistics award, then this was a fee extracted from a client government rather than a rail, and the analogy should be marked down accordingly.

lecture.title: The Economic Weapon: Why Sieges Make the Wars They Mean to Prevent

sections.t: Treasury designated roughly sixty Chinese “teapot” refiners — the small plants buying discounted Iranian crude — while touching no Chinese state major and no bank. The same week, central banks bought a record 288.9 tonnes of gold in the quarter gold fell over 20%. Two stories, one machine.

sections.h: Follow the money, name the mechanism
sections.t: A reserve manager buying into a 20% drawdown is not trading. He is hedging ACCESS — the risk that an asset held abroad gets switched off by its host government — and gold is the only large reserve asset with no counterparty who can flip that switch. Name the mechanism: the ECONOMIC WEAPON, using the financial plumbing whose hubs one country owns to inflict a siege without laying one. Iran discounts crude to Chinese teapots paying through dollar-touching chains; Treasury designates them; the IRGC's Strait Authority recoups the shortfall in Hormuz tolls. Sanction and gold bar are one transaction seen from two ends.

sections.h: Deep history I — the blockade that became an idea
sections.t: The economic weapon has a birthday and a founding failure. The birthday is November 1806, when Napoleon's Berlin Decrees declared the British Isles blockaded — the Continental System, an attempt to beat a maritime power by closing a continent's markets to it. It succeeded at nothing except generating enforcement. Portugal would not comply, so France invaded in 1807 and got the Peninsular War, the ulcer that bled the Grande Armée for six years. Alexander I quit the system in December 1810 because it was ruining Russian trade, and in 1812 Napoleon marched east to enforce it. The blockade never defeated Britain; it manufactured the two wars that destroyed the blockader. Sanctions require enforcement, and enforcement against a determined leakage path tends toward conquest. The second case mattered because it worked. The Allied blockade of Germany ran from 1914 through the armistice and was lifted only when Germany signed at Versailles in June 1919. German official estimates put civilian deaths from malnutrition near 424,000 — contested, and historians still argue how much was blockade and how much German agricultural mismanagement. But perception makes policy, and a generation concluded hunger had beaten an undefeated army. So they institutionalized it as a PEACE instrument: Article 16 of the League Covenant made sanctions automatic against an aggressor, and Wilson in 1919 put it in words no Treasury official would dare use today — “A nation that is boycotted is a nation that is in sight of surrender. Apply this economic, peaceful, silent, deadly remedy and there will be no need for force.” The weapon was invented to ABOLISH war; the rest of the century refutes that sentence.

sections.h: Deep history II — the failures that define our problem
sections.t: ABYSSINIA, 1935. Italy invaded Ethiopia; the League invoked Article 16 — exempting oil, coal and steel, and never closing the Suez Canal, which Britain controlled and through which Italian troopships sailed. Mussolini won anyway. The sanctions were real enough to enrage and too porous to stop, and the lesson is sharper than “sanctions don't work”: a sanction calibrated to spare the sender teaches the target that the sender is deterred too. Then the second-order effect. Nicholas Mulder's argument in The Economic Weapon is that the interwar regime deterred small states and PROVOKED large ones. Italy, Germany and Japan drew the same conclusion from the 1930s — dependence on seaborne trade was a vulnerability an enemy could switch off at will, and the answer was autarky, self-sufficiency taken by force. Lebensraum and the Co-Prosperity Sphere were ideological projects; they were also sanctions-proofing programs. Japan is the proof case. Washington embargoed scrap iron in 1940, then froze Japanese assets on 26 July 1941; America supplied roughly 80% of Japan's oil, and with Britain and the Dutch East Indies following, Japan lost about 88% of its oil imports. Reserves would last three years at peace, half that at war — Nagano's image was of a patient wasting away, every month of compliance leaving Japan weaker against the enemy it expected to fight. Pearl Harbor came in December. And the detail that turns story into discipline: the freeze was never meant to be total. Roosevelt intended a licensing regime keeping oil flowing so the tap stayed usable as leverage; officials in State and Treasury administered it so strictly that no licences issued and the flow stopped. The sanction that helped produce Pearl Harbor was substantially an organizational outcome, not a presidential decision — Allison's Essence of Decision, live. Before inferring “Iran's strategy” from one action, ask which bureau took it.

sections.h: The pattern — and where it breaks
sections.t: The leakage path is always the whole story — not the designation list, the leak: Portugal and Russia in 1806, Beira and Pretoria in 1966, Chinese teapots now. NOW THE BREAK. Japan in 1941 had a military option that promised to SOLVE its resource problem: seize the Dutch East Indies and own the oil. Iran has none — it fought its war, lost the conventional exchange, and has played its asymmetric card, the Hormuz toll. Nor did 1914 face an alternative supplier: Iran's is the world's second-largest economy, which the sanctioner just spared. Less Pearl Harbor, more Rhodesia.

MULDER says the siege provokes: strangulation drives large states to autarky, then preemption. DREZNER says sanctions are cheap theater — Hufbauer's data give a third success rate at best, near zero against great powers. The 2026 evidence buries neither: it splits by SIDE, and the split is the finding. On the TARGET Mulder scores: gold, stockpiles, payment rails, enrichment acceleration under maximum pressure. On the SENDER Drezner scores harder — the carve-outs. Sixty teapots and not one bank is not escalation; it is the sanctioner taking its own threat hostage, because hitting a Chinese bank endangers the dollar system that makes the hammer heavy.

The 2015 architecture is not coming back (high confidence): the 2022 freeze of Russian reserves turned the settlement network into an instrument; a hedge once bought is not resold. Expect bifurcation, not de-dollarization (moderate-high). EICHENGREEN is right that currencies erode glacially; the WEAPON depreciates faster than the CURRENCY. The bolder call (moderate): the most dangerous decade is the one in which the weapon still works but no longer terrifies. Mulder's mechanism fires in the transition — invested in escaping, not finished, expecting strangulation regardless. For China, the 2030s — so Economic D-Day may SHORTEN the fuse it was meant to lengthen. FALSIFIER: designate a major Chinese state bank; if Beijing cuts Iranian purchases within a quarter, I am wrong. Two centuries say the economic weapon does not replace war — it sorts the world into blocs that survive each other's sieges, then gives the survivors a reason to fight.

Nicholas Mulder, The Economic Weapon (2022) — published weeks before the Russia sanctions matched its template. Farrell & Newman, “Weaponized Interdependence” (2019) — it called the 2022 playbook and the chip controls in advance. Eichengreen, Exorbitant Privilege — the counterweight.

Nothing this afternoon adds to it - logged so the fire is dated once and not re-counted.
NOT fired, and it is the limit of the above: the hulls are Saudi and South Korean, not US-flagged. No confirmed American deaths, no struck US hull. The intercepted-volley equilibrium has not broken.

NOT fired, checked and logged so the non-fire is scoreable: no blocking designation on a top-ten Chinese bank; no Kremlin acceptance of any limited ceasefire; no ferry requisition, reserve mobilization or missile dispersal near Taiwan; no summit-cancellation signal; no verified IRGC or Basij defection; no strike on Kharg's loading terminals; no awarded dredging or terminal contract in Venezuela.

WIRE HYGIENE - a gap this board just found in itself. A new wire is written and armed below rather than pretended to have fired.

NEW - Venezuela: an awarded, funded dredging contract or a dedicated heavy-crude terminal tender in the Orinoco or Lake Maracaibo channel. This is the single observable that separates opportunistic spoils from a pre-built heavy-barrel rail, and it is what GEO-022 resolves on
A struck US-flagged hull or a confirmed American death - the falsifier on the whole intercepted-volley equilibrium, and still the only escalation trigger left unfired in the strait

A war-risk re-rating of the southern Hormuz corridor by the Joint War Committee, or a withdrawal of the US clearance claim - the actuarial event that governs GEO-001 far more than any diplomatic announcement
A strike on Kharg's LOADING terminals as opposed to its military sites - it would convert the Aug 30 video from theatre into a warning order and re-rate GEO-001, GEO-003 and GEO-009 together
A failed or heavily tailed JGB or gilt auction - the point at which the long-end repricing stops being a price move and becomes a funding event

Scholar-owned: IRGC/Basij defection (Takeyh) - casualty-recruitment crossover (Kofman) - PLA purge tempo (Fravel)

watch: Whether an American is killed or a US-flagged hull is struck. It remains the published trigger on this board and it remains unfired - Jordan intercepted 10 of 13 missiles with the rest landing in unpopulated ground, and the two hulls hit in the strait this week were Saudi and South Korean

Whether Jordan, Kuwait or Bahrain says anything publicly about the salvos they are absorbing. Iran has moved the physical cost of its retaliation onto three third countries, and the first host government to restrict US strike operations from its soil would be a larger event than any sortie count

Whether Berlin publishes an evidentiary basis or produces a suspect before the Bonn consulate general closes. Attribution without a named defendant is a policy instrument, and the European base rate since 2024 is expulsions and sanctions listings, never an Article 4 consultation

Whether the EPA issues a fuel-specification or blending waiver, or anyone in the administration raises distillate export limits. That, not a refiner meeting, is the instrument that moves American diesel - and it moves it by exporting the shortage to Europe and Latin America

The published Venezuela legal text before Chris Wright's arrival and the expected Chevron signing: governing law, arbitration seat, named sanctions authorisation, and whether the National Assembly members who approved the treaty are shown what they approved
